ety.text: From Middle English dich, from Old English dīċ (“trench, moat”) from Proto-Germanic *dīkaz (compare Swedish dike, Icelandic díki, West Frisian dyk (“dam”), Dutch dijk (“dam”), German Teich (“pond”)), from Proto-Indo-European *dʰeygʷ- (“to stick, set up”) (compare Latin fīgō (“to affix, fasten”), Lithuanian diegti (“to prick; plant”), dýgsti (“to geminate, grow”)). Doublet of dike.

senses.d: A trench; a long, shallow indentation, as for irrigation or drainage.
ex: Digging ditches has long been considered one of the most demanding forms of manual labor.
The truck careered off the road into a ditch.

senses.d: A raised bank of earth and the hedgerow on top.
ex:
You flung a ditch on my vision
Of beauty, love and truth.
O stony grey soil of Monaghan
You burgled my bank of youth!

senses.d: To discard or abandon; to stop associating with (someone).
ex: Once the sun came out we ditched our rain-gear and started a campfire.
Why did you ditch your last boyfriend? He was so nice to you.

senses.d: To deliberately crash-land an airplane on water.
ex: When the second engine failed, the pilot was forced to ditch; their last location was just south of the Azores.

senses.d: To deliberately not attend classes; to play hookey.
ex: The truant officer caught Louise ditching with her friends, and her parents were forced to pay a fine.
"No, instead, it just had enough power to transform me, overload, and force me to wait to change back! I had to ditch school!"
Enclosure led to fuller winter employment in hedging and ditching.
The soldiers ditched the tent to prevent flooding.
The engine was ditched and turned on its side.

ety.text: Literally, “make school (hidden) in bushes”. Where the idiom comes from is quite unclear. * It could be related to buissonner (verb), and metaphorically going on an adventure in the forest among shrubs and bushes instead of attending school.
